results.translation:
...hot and dry. And by these signs one shall recognize him: he has a pale complexion, like ashes, and this means that the fluid (moisture) has been consumed in him by the heat. He drinks more than he needs. As to his body, he is lean and yet has much flesh; his face is thin and gaunt, and he is quick to anger, though his anger passes quickly. He is swift in his deeds and is bold and quick in all his undertakings; he has no restraint in his speech, and he does not forget (grudges). He has a hard heart, yet he is generous, and does not consider to whom he gives. His worth lies in his heart, and his bones are coarse, as are his veins. He is quick and brisk and not sluggish. He desires women eagerly, but cannot manage much [with them]. Thus one may recognize the choleric type.

The phlegmatic resembles water and winter, for he is cold and moist, and these are his signs: he is pale/white in complexion, corpulent, and suffers from sluggish limbs, because he has no heat in him. He is soft and willingly obedient; he is fearful and not bold, and is not cheerful. He eats much and drinks little, and is slow in his affairs; he has soft hair and does not desire many women, yet he can manage much [with them], because he is cold — and naturally all women are cold and moist. And therefore a wise physician who [treats] wounds...

[The physician] wishing to treat must be careful that he recognize the nature and complexion of the person, that he know whether the person has a clear [pure] or soft, growing body, as children and some women do, and [whether he has] a moist temperament; to such clear and moist flesh belongs a drying medicine, because the body is moist. He should also observe whether the person has a dry body and flesh, as a person around forty years of age does, and also those who labor much and travel much are naturally dry in body; to such a one he must give a very drying medicine. And sometimes it happens that the moist nature becomes dry, and the dry becomes moist; in this matter the physician must be very careful that he go from one medicine to another according to how he observes the person, so that he does not make the moist dry, nor the dry moist, nor the hot cold, nor the cold hot. Also some members of a person are of a much drier nature than others, such as the bones [?] and the [artery/vessel?], and therefore they need a stronger drying medicine than the others. [The] ... is much different in the person than [the rest].

And therefore every physician should be diligent when he wishes to produce granulation (proud flesh) and fresh flesh in the wound, so that he prepares the medicine according to the nature and complexion of the person, and especially in wounds that do not readily wish to heal. You should note that there are many kinds of wounds that befall people, such as stabbed, cut, struck, shot, or from falling. And in all these and other wounds a physician should be careful: some wounds are to be sewn, and the seam should be neat, and he should be skillful and quick about it; and some wounds are not to be sewn — those he should leave alone according to his art. Also note that some wounds are mortal, some are harmful but long-lasting (curable over time), and some are harmful but not long-lasting. The mortal wounds are such as when the heart is wounded, and the stomach, and the bladder, and the liver, and other internal organs of the person; and whoever is wounded in the head such that the brain comes out — in all such wounds God the Lord is the best physician. When the belly is wounded in such a way that it swells or bulges and festers, or that the fire [fever] takes hold of it — that is death.

The stab-wounds and lame (paralyzing) wounds are all wounds where there is not much flesh and many sinews; and these are the wounds of the hands and the bones (limbs), and of the running (tendons) and of the joints, and of the sinews and of the hair-wash [hamstring?], which are called 'lacerti,' and four fingers above the knee and four fingers below, and near the ankle. If the bones are struck off or broken there, that is all stab-like and lame, and sometimes deadly.

When such a wound befalls a person, he readily falls into unrest so that he cannot sleep, and he cramps up, with great pain; and also the cramp comes to the wound, above all wounds upon a person and travels [spreads]. It is useful and good for the doctor to give the person a stool [purgative/laxative? or a specific remedy] made for this, so that the bad vapors/humors do not settle at the wound and corrupt it further.

And for falling wounds that recur to a person, the doctor should bring forth and prepare an emetic and a purgative from the stomach, from above.

And if it happens that a great flow [of blood] from a bone-wound occurs, then heal only the wound and let the bone alone; otherwise, if you wish to heal the bone but not the wound, then the person may get spasm — that is, cramp [convulsion].

results.translation:
How much blood there be, whether much or little, and all great wounds that need [treatment].

The harmful wounds on limbs — that is, all fresh wounds — require only a strong, pain-relieving [remedy] together with a common medicine that belongs to it; and all fresh wounds require more of a dry medicine, while the small ones never [need it]. It is reported that all wounds require dry medicine, except only the wounds of the belly, which cannot tolerate it. In all deep, straight, long or short wounds you should be diligent to fit the lips of the wound well together; and if they need stitching, then stitch them. And the deep ones you should heal from the bottom up, so that nothing unclean or full of pus remains within, unhealed. Also note that all wounds which appear healed but still have matter (pus) inside must be cut open again, so that the pus and the impurity flow out. How you should cut — that is taught by the size of the wound and its nature. You should know that there is no better medicine for all wounds than good wine. Warm wine draws out the pus very quickly, as Hippocrates says, for wine renews and strengthens nature; and nature makes good flesh in man, and good flesh produces good blood, for there is no greater source in all wound medicine than this.

results.translation: [When] nature is robbed of its blood and the doctor cannot bring it back again, it is therefore necessary that the doctor come to the aid of the wounded man with good food, that is natural for him, and with good wine, so that nature may return and the sick person may again gain good, fresh, natural flesh and blood. And also above all things the wounded man should guard himself against unchastity and against shame with women, for shame brings desire, and desire brings deeds [works of the flesh]. You should also note that when nature does not have good food and good drink to make good flesh and fresh blood, then you can do nothing—neither with the clamp [splint] nor with the great wounds—by way of work or effect. Therefore a wise doctor should know the diet needed by the wounded patient, and feed him accordingly so that he may gain fresh, new, raw flesh and blood. And he should give him the food in moderation, according to the time of day. He should also take care that he does not give the patient food mixed with food that is not useful to him, so that nature is not hindered and the doctor's work is not prolonged. The foods that make good blood for him are good hens, capons, [and] young chickens.

results.translation: Good meat: young swan meat, partridge, pheasant, lamb, wild fowl, and good soup made from old hens, and good fresh eggs beaten into water and cooked therein — such and other good foods. A drink should be good old white wine. And moreover, for everyone whose wound is severe, the food and regimen should be adapted according to his nature; that is, for him the harmful remedies [should be avoided], and especially in the case of women. The species [remedies/simples] for wounds that are cold and hot, and that dry out the [wound near the] nose, are: henbane seed, mandrake, and celery/parsley. Of these every physician should beware, for although it is true that they dry the wounds very much, they nevertheless cool the wounds excessively. Also beware of resin — that is, of pine-pitch and black pitch — for these are excessively hot; you should not place them on a fresh wound unless you have first mixed them with a cooling remedy. Also note: if the air is cold, then give a hot remedy; but if it is hot, then give a cold remedy. Also note the remedies that generate flesh and produce it, as Galen says: that is, frankincense, barley flour and bean [flour], vetch, iris, mugwort plant, opopanax, and [thuria?] — and these are, some more drying, some less; some have a simple power, some a compounded power, for [continues]...

You should purge the whole body of the wounded man with medicine (pharmacy), as [follows]. In all wounds that bleed in moderation, you should not stop [the bleeding], for it may be that it wants to bleed too much; for a moderately excessive flow of blood is healthy for the wound. But the excessive flow of blood one should not stop entirely, for it may be that the [morbid] matter comes to the place and departs from it; but one should close and stop up the hollow of the veins. But when a person turns himself this way and that, or when his body — the cold and the healthy part — moves the wounded limb, then the blood is halted; and for this a cold drink of water is also very useful for a person who bleeds very strongly. But when one binds the wound very well and tightly together, that also helps well. And for all fluxes of blood there is nothing better than to do this: take white wax [egg white?], and red [wax?], and mastic; chew these with the teeth so that they become like a paste (mush), and lay this upon the wound, and over it a sponge, and bind it. Or make this remedy: take one part mastic and one part aloe, make it into a paste with the white of an egg, and then take hare's hair and put it in, and mix it thoroughly, and use it as needed.

From the uppermost [part] down to the lowest, and again from the lowest up to the uppermost, as we do on the veins of the hands and the feet: if a vein or one that is standing (prominent) is wounded, then you cannot stanch the blood in any other way than by binding the vein very tightly, or by opening a vein on the same [limb] and letting it bleed, and you should bind it well at both ends and then let it stand still. This is a good remedy for the wound of a vein or artery, which are the channels of life and [it] is strong and good. One should take hare's hair, cut it small with a knife, and mix it with the powder made from aloes; and add sandarac or bolus armenicus, and temper all of this together with white ant-eggs (?), and mix it so that the lime becomes like honey, and lay that upon the wounded vein as written above.

I have seen many where the healing of the skin was not accomplished properly, and this was because the doctor could not recognize the wound and not only [treat it] with [poultice/ointment] and warmth, when it appears that the skull bone is fractured, so that it seems just like a small crack that cannot be recognized. And [to know] whether the skull is neither lower nor higher than it was before, you should [do the following] to recognize this: close the person's mouth and nostrils very tightly and tell him to blow hard, and if the breath comes right to the crack, then know that the skull bone is cracked or fissured. Then dab [a remedy] and spread it on the wound and let it dry, and where you then see a crack, that same thing is the skull bone being cracked. The remedy for this is: if the wound is narrow, make it wide, because otherwise the flow of blood will hinder you. So take [an instrument/probe] and press on both sides evenly at the wound's opening, and afterward take a file (rasp) and file the wound open from one side of the opening to the other, and afterward when you see the wound, clean it carefully with a clean cloth [to remove] the membrane of the brain [dura mater].

Concerning the wound-matter (pus) that has formed over time and must afterward heal in every way as has been written before; however, it is better that one make a wider opening so that the pus can be pressed out, and its strength holds itself back naturally. Master Rogerius says: take saffron and mix it into water and let it soak in there for a good while, so that the water turns yellow. Afterward strain it and put wheat flour into that water and let it simmer a little, stirring it with a piece of wood, and keep it. You may well spread this ointment onto the wound at first, for it takes away the pain; and at the last, apply the ointment 'apostolicon' spread on leather to close the wound.

Master Hugo says: it often happens that the head becomes bruised and often swollen and puffy, and often swells much and often little, however it may be — take then flax-tow (or wool) and moisten it, and take it mixed with salt and bind that onto the head, and let it lie there for three days; and if the swelling and the pain of the head do not diminish, then shave the head and lay the poultice/plaster upon it.

You make it thus: take good wine and put into it salt that has been well pulverized, and let it come to a good boil in a pan, and afterward put the powder into it.

This is a healing (treatment) for wounds. But if it is torn to the bone and hangs down with the skin, then stitch it up and proceed in all things as written above; and when you have stitched the wound, lay the red powder upon it, made as follows. How to make the red powder:
Take greater comfrey (consolida maior) one drachm, bole (bolus) one drachm, dried peppercorns three drachms, mastic-gum an equal amount, ceruse (white lead) an equal amount, [and] two drachms of dragon's blood — grind all these to powder and keep it. This powder stops the blood and heals the flesh at the seam after stitching, and forms good skin over the wound. And when you have stitched the wound and applied the powder upon it, then lay at the end of the wound a plantain leaf or a compress, and afterward a poultice-cloth over that, so that the matter (pus) that flows out from the place of the wound is drawn off. And apply the powder twice each day upon the wound, and do this each day until you see the flesh grow and heal; then draw the threads out of the stitched wound, and afterward heal it with a plaster as written above. And in the seam of the wound that has been made by the physician (surgeon), lay a dry cloth on it, and so heal it as before. You should know that one leaves the threads at the stitching of a wound on the head in the wound for eight days, and otherwise [differently for other places].

Concerning the wounds of the belly and how they are to be sewn together, you should note that the place on the body that is soft is called the belly (paunch), and it is made of two skins (layers): one above, which is coarse, and one below, which is very soft, and is called 'amoritta' (?); after this there are two more, called 'lacerti' (little muscles), which are hair-fine, full of sinews and very thin, just like a sieve, and are joined together in such a way that they cannot be separated; and above this one thinks it is only a single skin of the belly, though there is no more. After this come two muscles ('lacerti') which have flesh, going down from the chest to the bone of the chest, and one is always joined to the other; and this is called 'myrach' (the diaphragm/muscle layer). And after this there is a little membrane ('hewtlein') that surrounds the whole belly, and is called the peritoneum, and has no blood, and is full of sinews; and this is sewn together from the right side.

results.translation: But if the other intestines are wounded, then take a little tube or a hollow reed that is as thick and as wide as the wounded intestine, and scrape it and make it as thin as [needed] so that it can be grasped, and let the tube also be longer than the wound is. Then push the tube into the wounded intestine and let the tube protrude well on both sides. Sew the wound shut in this way with a silk thread, and afterward clean the intestine of the excrement that comes out entirely, with a clean and small piece of lint moistened in warm wine. And when it is now quite clean, then put it back in again and arrange it so that it lies in its [proper] place and is laid [back]. After that, sew the wound of the belly, as I have taught before, and let the wound of the belly not remain open, as master Rogerius and Rynald once taught. If the wound of the belly stood open, then the sickness could bring much harm and pain thereafter, because the air would go in, and the doctor would have much trouble before he healed the wound. And another thing is that flies would notice the wound and the intestines would go out [i.e., prolapse], and therefore sew the wound and keep the sick person warm with good wine, and the sick person should always lie so that the wound is uppermost, and also take care of the sick person that nothing further [happens] to the wounded intestine.

As often as in the arm the bones, or the same bone or other limb is broken, the physician should be very quick and should, when he arranges the break, see to it that no fragment of the broken bone lies upon another; for if fragments of a broken bone lie upon one another, the physician should then straighten the tissue and strengthen the flesh, and should with his hand handle and manipulate the broken bone in such a way that the break fits together and stands right, as with a whole bone. After that, the physician should take blood from the skin of the bone (limb) and smear the break and the bone with it, and afterward with honey. After that he should take the whites of eight eggs or more and beat them in a bowl with a spoon until it foams very well, and make of it a plaster on a cloth that is as long as needed so that it can go around the bone at the break, and also as wide that it can well cover the break, so that the egg white soaks through it; then lay this upon the break and thereby treat the break, and take a bandage that is neither too long nor too wide, and (wrap it) fairly firmly, so that it does not shift the break.

Taken on an empty stomach, it cures dropsy together with fevers, and heals daily (quotidian) fevers, harming nothing. One should drink of this water to be cured; and if there is blood mixed with choleric or phlegmatic humor, it moves it quickly. This same water, taken with dropsy on an empty stomach, removes head-fever and pain, and makes a man sleep well; digestion improves, and it likewise removes hair for a long time from a place, and diminishes swelling(?).
